final_recommendation: The room converged on a labor enforcement amendment framework (day-91 automatic tariffs, advisory arbiter, co-inspector joint reports) that Mexico committed to deliver in binding text by Friday. Congress agreed to review the text Friday afternoon and, if those three elements are confirmed, announce a January floor vote that same day. Canada locked its red line: labor enforcement only, no reopening of dairy or Chapter 19. The deal is contingent on Friday's text matching the verbal commitments.
minority_objections: Labor union initially pushed for day-15 tariff accrual, which Mexico rejected as crossing sovereignty lines
Business lobby pressed for immediate public floor-vote commitment before text review, which Congress refused
key_conflicts: Congress vs. Mexico on tariff trigger timing (day-15 vs. day-91)
Congress vs. Mexico on arbiter authority (neutral third party vs. Mexican labor body)
Business/media vs. Congress on timing of public announcement (immediate vs. post-text-review)
Labor union vs. Mexico on inspector authority scope (stop-facility-mid-shift vs. observation-and-reporting)
key_concessions: Mexico accepted co-inspector joint reports and day-91 automatic tariffs (moved from initial resistance to facility inspections)
Congress accepted Mexican labor body as arbiter (moved from demanding neutral third party)
Congress accepted day-91 timeline (moved from labor's day-15 demand)
Mexico accepted that arbiter decision is advisory only and cannot reset tariff clock
Congress agreed to announce January vote same-day Friday if text confirms (moved from withholding signal until markup)
red_lines: Canada: amendment must be labor enforcement only; any reopening of dairy or Chapter 19 triggers Canadian withdrawal
Mexico: day-91 tariff trigger is final; no day-15 accrual or neutral arbiter with binding authority
Congress: tariffs must be automatic on day-91 with no arbiter reset; co-inspectors must file joint reports
Labor union: tariffs execute on day-91 regardless of arbiter finding, or no vote
Mexico: no amendments after Friday text is tabled
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: What happens if co-inspectors cannot agree on a joint report (not just remediation assessment)
Operational details of how Mexican labor body arbiter is selected and insulated from political pressure
Enforcement gap if Mexico's labor body finds remediation adequate but U.S. unions/Congress disagree after day-91 tariffs land
Timeline risk: Friday text delivery, same-day Congressional review, and same-day public announcement is extremely compressed
Domestic Canadian opposition to the labor amendment itself (Canada focused only on preventing reopening of other chapters)
What constitutes 'measurable remediation' in binding legal terms beyond verbal assurances
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Friday's binding text actually contains the three locked elements in enforceable legal language
Whether Congress's Friday afternoon review identifies gaps not surfaced in this meeting
Whether Congress actually announces January vote Friday evening or finds new conditions
Whether business coalition mobilizes for ratification before seeing operational proof of enforcement
Whether labor union members accept Mexican labor body as legitimate arbiter
Whether Canadian domestic opposition emerges to the labor amendment framework itself
Whether Mexico's government can deliver binding Protocol text by Friday given domestic legislative process
Whether January floor vote timeline holds if markup reveals enforcement ambiguities
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved verbal convergence on enforcement mechanics but has not seen binding legal text. Congress's same-day Friday announcement is contingent on text review confirming the three elements, creating a tight timeline with no buffer for ambiguity. The arbiter framework (Mexican labor body, advisory only, 14-day window) was accepted under pressure but its operational legitimacy with U.S. labor and enforceability in disputes remains untested. Canada's red line (labor only) is clear, but whether the amendment text itself might trigger Canadian domestic opposition was not explored. The definition of 'measurable remediation' and the process if co-inspectors cannot agree on a joint report remain unresolved.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress opened with 'I've got the votes to kill this thing' and the entire meeting was structured around whether the package could pass as-is (it could not) or required amendment to secure votes. This was the central organizing question.
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Labor enforcement mechanism (facility inspections, tariff triggers, arbiter authority) drove every round. Congress stated 'my caucus won't move unless we get enforceable labor language' and the room spent all eight rounds negotiating enforcement teeth.
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business lobby pressed for certainty and floor-vote timeline ('every week we sit here is another week our members don't invest') and demanded public commitment, but did not dominate the room's direction—enforcement mechanics did.
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada's dairy concession was mentioned only as a red line against reopening ('Canada will not reopen our dairy settlement'). It did not drive the discussion; Canada's role was defensive boundary-setting, not active negotiation.
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexico resisted neutral arbiter and day-15 tariffs as sovereignty violations ('Mexico's inspectors don't answer to a U.S.-appointed panel chair'), but accepted compromise (Mexican labor body, day-91). Present and real, but not the dominant driver—enforcement adequacy was.
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media actor pressed for public announcement timing and framed silence as doubt ('that silence reads as doubt'), but this was secondary to the substantive enforcement negotiation. Media shaped messaging strategy, not core deal terms.
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: The room treated the original package as unratifiable without amendment. Congress: 'current text is unenforceable'; Mexico: 'you're not getting ratification, you're getting a corpse' without negotiation. Stability required domestic-ratification compromise, which drove the entire meeting.
